title: The Helen Keller story doesn't add up
full_text:
Was Helen Keller a fraud? I've wondered
about that for over a decade, but I
really hesitated to make this video
because we live in an era that just
loves knocking down historical figures.
And I just don't think that's a good
idea to dismiss amazing people because
they held some outdated beliefs. I mean,
you can pick any hero and somebody's out
there with a takedown video on YouTube.
But this one's different [music] because
the question about Helen Keller isn't
about whether she was a bad person. It's
about whether her accomplishments were
even real. Whether the books, the
essays, the political philosophy
attributed to her actually came from her
mind or someone else's. The elephant in
the room is that the skeptics might have
a point.
I'm Ken Lacorte.
I dig into topics like this that make
some people uncomfortable and I try to
give you the fairest overview I can. And
I did my best here. In this video, we'll
first look at the legend of Helen
Keller, then take a quick look at
exactly what Keller's condition was.
Then ask, why don't we see that many
more Helen Keller's? Because we just

And finally, we'll try to figure out
whose words were really published. Okay.
So, the legend of Helen Keller starts in
Alabama where she was born in 1880. At
19 months old, an illness took her sight
and her hearing. For the next 5 years,
she lived in near total isolation,
unable to communicate beyond a few crude
gestures to her family. Then Anne
Sullivan showed up and the story that
followed became one of the most famous
in American history. Within weeks,
Keller was learning words through finger
spelling into her palm. By age 10, she
could read Braille in English, French,
and German.
By her teens, she was writing essays
that drew serious literary attention.
And along with Anne Sullivan, she was
world-famous for her whole life. Keller
became friends with Alexander Graham
Bell, Edison, Ford, Einstein, Chaplin,
Twain. She met 13 presidents. She
graduated from Radcliffe, Harvard's
women's college, with Sullivan at her
side interpreting lectures into her
hand. She was the first known deaf-blind
person to earn a bachelor's degree
anywhere. Keller wrote 14 books and
hundreds of essays and letters. She used
her fame as a political activist, a
suffragist, a socialist, a co-founder of
the ACLU, a vocal opponent of World War
I, and one of the earliest advocates for
people with disabilities. By any
measure, disabled or not, her resume is
extraordinary. That all stemmed from her
life story and her extraordinary
writing. By age 10, her letters became
remarkably sophisticated. She began
using flowery, somewhat Victorian
language that was very adult-like,
including visual descriptions and
metaphors that made her seem almost
supernatural to the public. In a poem
she wrote at 13, she described the
golds, scarlets, and purples of an
autumn landscape. Or she would write
about how she would delight in the
gorgeous colors of a sunset. She
described lilac, her teacher's favorite
color, as making her think of faces she
had loved and kissed. Gray was like a
soft shawl around the shoulders. Yellow
meant life and was rich in promise. All
that from a young woman who'd been blind
since she was 19 months old. When
critics challenged that visual language,
Keller responded that a blind person
should be allowed to use words whose
meaning one can only guess from analogy.
When a reviewer in The Nation called all
her knowledge hearsay knowledge, Keller
fired back that the bulk of the world's
knowledge is an imaginary construction.

nothing, the brain needs to build from

totally deaf-blind, but we only have the
judgment of doctors from a different

But her output never came close to

or political work of any sophistication.
There's a consistent pattern that the
earlier and that the more total the

notes.note: Polly Thomson wasn't a new hire after Sullivan's death. She joined the Keller-Sullivan household in 1914, working as secretary/housekeeper for 22 years before Sullivan died in 1936, then gradually became Keller's primary companion.
notes.claim: Polly Thompson had no background in literature or politics.
notes.context_quote: replaced by Polly Thompson, a woman with no background in literature or politics, and the output changed immediately.
notes.context_paragraph: Then Sullivan died when Keller was 56 and replaced by Polly Thompson, a woman with no background in literature or politics, and the output changed immediately.

sources.quote: On October 20, 1914, Thomson joined the household as secretary, eventually becoming Keller’s companion and interpreter following Sullivan’s death in 1936.
sources.explanation: Confirms Thomson joined the household in 1914 (22 years before Sullivan's death) and served as secretary before becoming the primary companion.

sources.quote: Thomson spent 46 years with Keller, just 3 fewer than Sullivan’s tenure with Keller.
sources.explanation: Supports the claim of a long-term tenure that began decades before Sullivan passed away.

sources.quote: In 1914, Sullivan's health began to fail, so a young woman from Scotland, Polly Thomson, was hired to keep house. Though she had no experience with deaf or blind people, Thompson progressed to working as a secretary, and eventually became a constant companion to Keller.
sources.explanation: Corroborates that Thomson was hired in 1914 as a housekeeper and secretary, long before she became Keller's primary companion.

notes.note: Anne Sullivan married John Macy in May 1905. Two of Keller's three books from her 20s—The Story of My Life and Optimism—were published in 1902-03, before that marriage, so they weren't written during the time Keller was with Sullivan and her husband.
notes.claim: Helen Keller published three books in her 20s while she was with Anne Sullivan and Sullivan's husband.
notes.context_quote: During the time Keller was with Sullivan and her husband, she published three books in her 20s.
notes.context_paragraph: During the time Keller was with Sullivan and her husband, she published three books in her 20s. At the age of 33, she published out of the dark, a sustained work of socialist argument.

sources.quote: On May 3, 1905, Sullivan married Harvard University instructor and literary critic John Albert Macy
sources.explanation: Confirms the date of Sullivan's marriage, supporting the claim that 1902-1903 publications preceded the marriage.
